title: Research Bite #64: The Student Grouping Study
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #64 covers the Education Endowment Foundation's 'The Student Grouping Study,' an EEF-funded evaluation conducted with University College London's Institute of Education. Across 97 schools (28 using mixed-attainment grouping, 69 using attainment sets), the study compared the maths progress and self-confidence of Year 7 and 8 students (ages 11-13) taught in mixed-attainment classes versus sets. On average, students in mixed-attainment settings made about one month less progress than those in sets, though disadvantaged and low-achieving pupils progressed similarly regardless of grouping. High-attaining students in mixed groups made roughly two months less progress than their setted peers, and mixed grouping was also linked to lower self-confidence among low-attainers -- while setting more reliably stretched high attainers. The EEF's own recommendation is not a blanket endorsement of setting: teachers in mixed-attainment classes should work deliberately to stretch high-attainers, and schools that do set should ensure specialist maths teachers aren't concentrated only in top sets.
points: The roughly one-month average progress gap favoring setting is a real but modest effect size -- large enough to matter at scale across a system, but not evidence that mixed-attainment teaching is broadly ineffective.

That disadvantaged and low-achieving students progressed similarly under either grouping model complicates a simple 'setting is better' or 'mixed is more equitable' narrative -- the effect is concentrated among high attainers, not spread evenly.

High-attaining students losing roughly two months of progress in mixed-attainment classes is the study's most actionable finding for schools currently using mixed grouping: it flags exactly which student group needs a deliberate stretch strategy.

The self-confidence finding -- mixed grouping lowering low-attainers' confidence -- cuts against a common justification for mixed-ability teaching (protecting weaker students from the stigma of low sets), suggesting that justification doesn't hold up empirically here.

The EEF's practical recommendation (stretch high-attainers in mixed classes; don't concentrate specialist teachers only in top sets) is deliberately not a simple 'switch to setting' verdict -- it targets the specific mechanisms behind the gap rather than the grouping model wholesale.
quotes: The Student Grouping Study is an evaluation report published by the Education Endowment Foundation in collaboration with University College London.
This research analyses how organising Year 7 and Year 8 students into either attainment-based sets or mixed-ability groups influences their mathematical progress and self-confidence.

The findings indicate that students in mixed-attainment settings generally made one month less progress than those in setted classes, though outcomes were similar for disadvantaged and low-achieving pupils.
Beyond academic performance, the report examines implementation costs, teaching quality, and the specific classroom experiences of different learner demographics.

Additionally, mixed grouping negatively impacted low-attainers' self-confidence and generally failed to adequately challenge high-attaining students, an area where setting proved noticeably more effective.
